initial_observation.demographics: A woman in her 30s with relapsing-remitting MS
initial_observation.encounter_context: Contacted neurological outpatient clinic due to new onset headache
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Presented with daily, pounding and pressing bilateral headache, evolving into right-sided occipital and retroorbital pain, sensitive to light and sounds, with isolated right cheek twitches; physical exam normal except hyper-reflexia in left arm
presenting_symptoms: isolated recurrent twitches in right cheek
known_prior_history: Right-sided ophthalmic zoster infection 2 months prior to headache onset
No vascular risk factors, migraine or other neurological/inflammatory condition

evidence_items.source_text: A woman in her 30s with natalizumab-treated MS contacted our neurological outpatient clinic due to a new onset headache that started 2 months after a right-sided ophthalmic zoster infection. She had no vascular risk factors, migraine or any other neurological or inflammatory condition and was not taking any other medication apart from natalizumab. She later reported having chickenpox in childhood.

Two months later, she experienced daily, pounding and pressing bilateral headache which, after 4 weeks, changed to a right-sided occipital and retroorbital pain and after another month ended spontaneously. At this stage, she presented to our neurological outpatient clinic. She had no fever but was sensitive to light and sounds. She also reported isolated recurrent twitches in her right cheek while experiencing the right sided headache; there was no postictal state.

Brain MRI including angiographic and gadolinium enhanced sequences, performed 4 months after the ophthalmic zoster infection, demonstrated the presence of subacute ischaemic changes in the right basal ganglia and the right cerebral peduncle. Narrowing of the supraclinoid segment of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) and the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and gadolinium enhancement in the vessel wall of the right ICA and ACA were noted (figure 1).

A lumbar puncture was performed including analyses of cell count, protein, lactate and glucose as well as a broad microbiological assay since the patient was under immunomodulating treatment. White (<0,003×109/L) and red (<0,0003×1012/L) cell count, glucose (3.6 mmol/L), lactate (1.8 mmol/L) and albumin (155 mg/L) were normal. CSF was positive for VZV-DNA. In serum, VZV IgG was positive, and IgM was at the threshold limit value.

All other virological and microbiological CSF and serum PCR investigations were negative (Herpes simplex virus-1 and -2, HHV-6, CMV, EBV, human parechovirus, enterovirus, Borrelia burgdorferi, Cryptococcus neoformans/gatti, Escherichia coli K1, H. influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptococcus pneumoniae). No test for JC virus was performed since there were no clinical signs of encephalopathy and the recent test was negative, 3 months prior to the examination at the outpatient clinic.

On admission, the patient was started on methylprednisolone intravenously 1 g once a day, acyclovir intravenously 750 mg three times per day and acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg once a day. After 3 days of methylprednisolone intravenously, she was switched to 50 mg once a day of orally administered prednisolone for 2 days with subsequent tapering of 10 mg per day.

Treatment with natalizumab was paused. The patient was asymptomatic during in-hospital stay and discharged home after 7 days. Acyclovir was administered intravenously until the follow-up lumbar puncture, when VZV-PCR DNA was negative. Virological and microbiological analyses as above were still negative. In serum, HbsAg, anti-HCV, HIV antibodies and antigen, Treponema pallidum and VZV IgM were negative. VZV IgG was positive, as before. The ratio of CD4+/CD8+ (2.65) as well as CD4 percentage (47%) and count (0.69 x 109 /L) were normal in whole blood.
Natalizumab treatment was terminated, and she was started on rituximab instead.

A follow-up MRI scan of the brain was performed 6 weeks after the MRI preceding hospitalisation and demonstrated persisting vasculitic vessel wall changes in the right ICA and the right ACA. Gadolinium enhancement was still present (see figure 1).

The next follow-up MRI scan of the brain was performed 9 months later, demonstrating regression of the gadolinium enhancement in the vessel walls, but persisting vessel wall thickening in the affected vessel segments. No new lesions were found.

Based on the radiological findings and in the context of the clinical symptom dynamics, lumbar puncture results and the absence of other toxic, renal, cardiac or other comorbidities, we strongly sustain the diagnosis of cerebral zoster vasculopathy.
